Name: crosslorauniversalmerging
Title: Universal Language Model Merging: Cross-LoRA Knowledge Injection for Multi-Domain MoE and Dense Architectures
Short Hypothesis: Can Cross-LoRA and knowledge injection techniques be effectively used to merge and transfer knowledge across multiple domains in both Dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models, leading to high performance and parameter interchangeability?
Related Work: Recent works such as 'Selective Knowledge Injection via Adapter Modules in Large-Scale Language Models' (Zheng et al., 2025) and 'WeaveRec: An LLM-Based Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation Framework with Model Merging' (Hou et al., 2025) have explored the use of adapter modules and model merging for knowledge injection and cross-domain adaptation. However, these studies primarily focus on specific domains or tasks and do not address the broader challenge of merging models with identical architectures across multiple domains. Our proposal extends these ideas by investigating the merging of both Dense and MoE architectures, ensuring parameter interchangeability and high performance across all domains.
Abstract: The recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated exceptional capabilities across diverse natural language processing tasks. However, training a single model to excel in multiple, specialized domains remains computationally expensive and challenging due to catastrophic forgetting and domain interference. In this proposal, we introduce a novel framework for **model weight merging** and **model weight transferring** restricted to the language modality. We focus on integrating knowledge from multiple domains into a unified model while ensuring that model parameters are interchangeable and achieve high performance across all targeted domains. Specifically, we investigate the merging of models with identical underlying architectures, evaluating both **Dense** and **Mixture-of-Experts (MoE)** networks. Our approach leverages **Cross-LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)** techniques to efficiently transfer and align domain-specific representations, coupled with targeted **knowledge injection** mechanisms to preserve and enhance domain expertise during the merging process. By exploring the dynamics of weight merging within the constraints of identical architectures, we aim to uncover generalizable principles for creating versatile, multi-domain language models without the need for extensive retraining from scratch. This research not only provides a scalable solution for building comprehensive AI systems but also contributes to our understanding of parameter interoperability and knowledge representation in both Dense and MoE language models.
Experiments: Experiment 1: **Cross-LoRA Initialization and Training** - Train separate Dense and MoE models on different domains (e.g., news, scientific articles, and social media). Apply Cross-LoRA to initialize adapter modules for each domain-specific model. Evaluate the performance of each model on domain-specific tasks to establish a baseline.

Experiment 2: **Knowledge Injection and Merging** - Use the trained adapter modules to inject domain-specific knowledge into a unified base model. Merge the adapter modules using a weighted averaging technique, ensuring that the merged model maintains high performance across all domains. Evaluate the merged model on a combination of tasks from all domains.

Experiment 3: **Parameter Interchangeability** - Test the interchangeability of the merged model parameters by swapping adapter modules between the Dense and MoE architectures. Measure the performance impact of parameter swapping to ensure that the merged model remains robust and adaptable.

Experiment 4: **Scalability and Efficiency** - Assess the computational efficiency and scalability of the merging process by varying the number of domains and the size of the adapter modules. Compare the resource requirements and performance of the merged model with that of training a single model from scratch.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Domain Interference: Merging models from vastly different domains may introduce interference, leading to degraded performance.
Parameter Interchangeability: Ensuring that adapter modules are interchangeable between Dense and MoE architectures may be challenging.
Computational Resources: The merging process, while more efficient than training from scratch, still requires significant computational resources.
Generalization: The merged model may not generalize well to unseen domains or tasks.

Name: crossmodalknowledgetransferforllms
Title: Cross-Modal Knowledge Transfer for Enhancing Multi-Modality in Large Language Models
Short Hypothesis: Can cross-modal knowledge transfer techniques be effectively applied to Large Language Models (LLMs) to enhance their multi-modality capabilities, specifically by leveraging visual and auditory data to improve text generation and understanding?
Related Work: Recent works such as 'CREST: Cross-modal Resonance through Evidential Deep Learning for Enhanced Zero-Shot Learning' (Huang et al., 2024) and 'Cross-Modal Knowledge Transfer Without Task-Relevant Source Data' (Ahmed et al., 2022) have explored cross-modal knowledge transfer in deep learning, primarily focusing on zero-shot learning and transferring knowledge from RGB to depth/infrared modalities. However, these studies do not address the integration of cross-modal knowledge into LLMs to enhance their multi-modality capabilities. Our proposal extends these ideas by investigating how visual and auditory data can be used to enrich the text generation and understanding abilities of LLMs.
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities in natural language processing tasks, but their performance in multi-modal settings remains limited. In this proposal, we explore the application of cross-modal knowledge transfer techniques to enhance the multi-modality capabilities of LLMs. Specifically, we aim to leverage visual and auditory data to improve text generation and understanding. By integrating cross-modal knowledge, we hypothesize that LLMs can better contextualize and generate text that is more aligned with visual and auditory inputs. This research not only aims to improve the performance of LLMs in multi-modal tasks but also contributes to a deeper understanding of how cross-modal information can be effectively integrated into language models.
Experiments: Experiment 1: **Cross-Modal Pretraining** - Pretrain a large language model using a dataset that includes aligned text, image, and audio pairs. Evaluate the model's ability to generate text that is contextually relevant to the visual and auditory inputs.

Experiment 2: **Cross-Modal Fine-Tuning** - Fine-tune the pretrained model on specific multi-modal tasks such as image captioning, audio-to-text transcription, and cross-modal retrieval. Compare the performance of the fine-tuned model with a baseline LLM trained only on text data.

Experiment 3: **Cross-Modal Attention Mechanisms** - Introduce cross-modal attention mechanisms to allow the model to dynamically attend to relevant visual and auditory features when generating text. Evaluate the impact of these mechanisms on the model's performance in multi-modal tasks.

Experiment 4: **Scalability and Efficiency** - Assess the computational efficiency and scalability of the cross-modal knowledge transfer process. Measure the resource requirements and performance gains of the enhanced LLM compared to a baseline model.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Data Alignment: Ensuring that the text, image, and audio data are accurately aligned can be challenging and may affect the quality of the pretrained model.
Model Complexity: Integrating cross-modal attention mechanisms may increase the complexity of the model, potentially leading to longer training times and higher computational costs.
Evaluation Metrics: Developing appropriate evaluation metrics for multi-modal tasks can be difficult, as it requires a balance between text quality and alignment with visual and auditory inputs.
Generalization: The enhanced LLM may not generalize well to unseen multi-modal tasks or data, especially if the training data is limited or biased.

Name: metalearningfewshotdomainadaptation
Title: Meta-Learning for Few-Shot Domain Adaptation in Natural Language Processing
Short Hypothesis: Can a meta-learning framework be developed to enable few-shot domain adaptation in natural language processing, specifically by leveraging adversarial domain adaptation and dynamic balance mechanisms to improve the model's ability to adapt to new tasks and domains?
Related Work: Recent works such as 'Meta-Learning Adversarial Domain Adaptation Network for Few-Shot Text Classification' (Han et al., 2021) and 'Few-shot multi-domain text intent classification with Dynamic Balance Domain Adaptation Meta-learning' (Yang et al., 2024) have explored the use of meta-learning and domain adaptation for few-shot learning in NLP. However, these studies primarily focus on specific tasks and datasets, and do not address the broader challenge of developing a generalizable meta-learning framework for few-shot domain adaptation across multiple domains. Our proposal extends these ideas by integrating adversarial domain adaptation and dynamic balance mechanisms to enhance the model's adaptability and generalization.
Abstract: Few-shot domain adaptation in natural language processing (NLP) remains a challenging task, particularly when dealing with limited labeled data and significant domain shifts. In this proposal, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework designed to enable few-shot domain adaptation in NLP. Our approach combines adversarial domain adaptation and dynamic balance mechanisms to improve the model's ability to adapt to new tasks and domains. By leveraging a meta-learning strategy, the model can rapidly learn from a few examples and generalize to unseen domains. We hypothesize that this framework will not only enhance the model's adaptability but also improve its performance on a variety of NLP tasks, such as text classification, sentiment analysis, and named entity recognition. This research aims to provide a scalable and effective solution for few-shot domain adaptation, contributing to the broader field of NLP and machine learning.
Experiments: Experiment 1: **Adversarial Domain Adaptation Pretraining** - Pretrain a meta-learning model using an adversarial domain adaptation network on a diverse set of NLP tasks and domains. Evaluate the model's ability to generate domain-invariant features and improve few-shot learning performance.

Experiment 2: **Dynamic Balance Fine-Tuning** - Fine-tune the pretrained model on specific few-shot tasks using a dynamic balance mechanism to adjust the importance of different domains during training. Compare the performance of the fine-tuned model with a baseline meta-learning model without dynamic balance.

Experiment 3: **Cross-Domain Evaluation** - Evaluate the fine-tuned model on a variety of cross-domain few-shot tasks, including text classification, sentiment analysis, and named entity recognition. Measure the model's performance in terms of accuracy, F1-score, and domain adaptation effectiveness.

Experiment 4: **Scalability and Efficiency** - Assess the computational efficiency and scalability of the meta-learning framework by varying the number of domains and the size of the training sets. Compare the resource requirements and performance gains of the proposed framework with existing methods.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Domain Shift: Significant differences between source and target domains may reduce the effectiveness of the meta-learning framework.
Data Availability: Limited labeled data in target domains may hinder the model's ability to adapt effectively.

Model Complexity: The integration of adversarial domain adaptation and dynamic balance mechanisms may increase the complexity of the model, potentially leading to longer training times and higher computational costs.
Generalization: The model may not generalize well to unseen tasks or domains, especially if the training data is biased or limited.

Name: selfsupervisedfewshotnlp
Title: Self-Supervised Learning for Few-Shot Domain Adaptation in NLP
Short Hypothesis: Can self-supervised learning techniques be effectively combined with few-shot domain adaptation to improve the performance of NLP models in low-resource and diverse domain scenarios?
Related Work: Recent works such as 'Self-Supervised Learning for Domain Adaptation in NLP' (Zhang et al., 2022) and 'Meta-Learning Adversarial Domain Adaptation Network for Few-Shot Text Classification' (Han et al., 2021) have explored the use of self-supervised learning and meta-learning for domain adaptation in NLP. However, these studies primarily focus on either self-supervised pretraining or meta-learning separately, and do not fully integrate both approaches to tackle the challenge of few-shot domain adaptation in low-resource settings. Our proposal aims to bridge this gap by combining self-supervised learning with few-shot domain adaptation to enhance model performance and generalization.
Abstract: Few-shot domain adaptation in natural language processing (NLP) remains a significant challenge, especially in low-resource settings where labeled data is scarce. In this proposal, we explore the integration of self-supervised learning techniques with few-shot domain adaptation to improve the performance of NLP models in diverse and low-resource domains. By leveraging self-supervised learning, we aim to pretrain models on large amounts of unlabeled data, enabling them to learn rich, domain-agnostic representations. These representations are then fine-tuned using few-shot domain adaptation techniques to adapt to specific tasks and domains with minimal labeled data. We hypothesize that this combined approach will not only enhance the model's ability to generalize to new tasks and domains but also improve its performance in low-resource scenarios. This research aims to provide a scalable and effective solution for few-shot domain adaptation, contributing to the broader field of NLP and machine learning.
Experiments: Experiment 1: **Self-Supervised Pretraining** - Pretrain a transformer-based NLP model using self-supervised learning techniques on a large corpus of unlabeled text data from diverse domains. Evaluate the pretrained model's performance on a set of benchmark NLP tasks to establish a baseline.

Experiment 2: **Few-Shot Domain Adaptation** - Fine-tune the pretrained model on specific few-shot tasks using a small amount of labeled data from different domains. Compare the performance of the fine-tuned model with a baseline model pretrained only on labeled data.

Experiment 3: **Cross-Domain Evaluation** - Evaluate the fine-tuned model on a variety of cross-domain few-shot tasks, including text classification, sentiment analysis, and named entity recognition. Measure the model's performance in terms of accuracy, F1-score, and domain adaptation effectiveness.

Experiment 4: **Scalability and Efficiency** - Assess the computational efficiency and scalability of the combined self-supervised and few-shot domain adaptation approach. Measure the resource requirements and performance gains of the proposed method compared to existing methods.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Data Quality: The quality of the unlabeled data used for self-supervised pretraining can significantly impact the model's performance.
Domain Shift: Significant differences between the pretraining and target domains may reduce the effectiveness of the few-shot domain adaptation.

Model Complexity: The integration of self-supervised learning and few-shot domain adaptation may increase the complexity of the model, potentially leading to longer training times and higher computational costs.
Generalization: The model may not generalize well to unseen tasks or domains, especially if the training data is limited or biased.

Name: contextualizedfewshotnlp
Title: Contextualized Few-Shot Learning for Cross-Domain Natural Language Processing
Short Hypothesis: Can contextualized few-shot learning techniques, combining advanced language embeddings with meta-learning, be effectively used to improve cross-domain performance in NLP tasks with minimal labeled data?
Related Work: Recent works such as 'A Survey on Few-Shot Learning in Natural Language Processing' (Yang, 2021) and 'Integrating Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning with Advanced Language Embeddings for Few-Shot Intent Classification' (Rahimi and Veisi, 2024) have explored the use of few-shot learning and meta-learning in NLP. However, these studies primarily focus on specific tasks and do not address the broader challenge of cross-domain few-shot learning. Our proposal extends these ideas by integrating contextualized embeddings and meta-learning to enhance cross-domain performance with minimal labeled data.
Abstract: Few-shot learning in natural language processing (NLP) is crucial for adapting models to new tasks and domains with limited labeled data. In this proposal, we introduce a novel framework for **contextualized few-shot learning** that combines advanced language embeddings with meta-learning techniques to improve cross-domain performance. By leveraging contextualized embeddings, such as BERT and LaBSE, we aim to capture rich, domain-agnostic representations that can be effectively adapted to new tasks and domains using few examples. Our approach integrates these embeddings with model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) to enable rapid adaptation and generalization. We hypothesize that this combined approach will not only enhance the model's ability to generalize to new tasks and domains but also improve its performance in low-resource scenarios. This research aims to provide a scalable and effective solution for few-shot cross-domain NLP, contributing to the broader field of NLP and machine learning.
Experiments: Experiment 1: **Contextualized Embedding Pretraining** - Pretrain a transformer-based NLP model using contextualized embeddings (e.g., BERT, LaBSE) on a large corpus of text data from diverse domains. Evaluate the pretrained model's performance on a set of benchmark NLP tasks to establish a baseline.

Experiment 2: **Meta-Learning Fine-Tuning** - Fine-tune the pretrained model using model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) on a few-shot dataset from a new domain. Compare the performance of the fine-tuned model with a baseline model pretrained only on labeled data.

Experiment 3: **Cross-Domain Evaluation** - Evaluate the fine-tuned model on a variety of cross-domain few-shot tasks, including text classification, sentiment analysis, and named entity recognition. Measure the model's performance in terms of accuracy, F1-score, and domain adaptation effectiveness.

Experiment 4: **Scalability and Efficiency** - Assess the computational efficiency and scalability of the combined contextualized embedding and meta-learning approach. Measure the resource requirements and performance gains of the proposed method compared to existing methods.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Data Quality: The quality of the pretraining data can significantly impact the model's performance.
Domain Shift: Significant differences between the pretraining and target domains may reduce the effectiveness of the few-shot adaptation.
Model Complexity: The integration of contextualized embeddings and meta-learning may increase the complexity of the model, potentially leading to longer training times and higher computational costs.
Generalization: The model may not generalize well to unseen tasks or domains, especially if the training data is limited or biased.
